title: How to sit: the body straight, the senses withdrawn (2.8–2.10)
hook: one of the oldest meditation instructions in India is about your spine, your breath, and choosing a quiet spot

segments.voice: Yesterday: the churning. Body as one fire stick, om as the other, back and forth until the hidden fire shows. Did you give something one more pull of the cord? Today, how to sit while you churn. Day four hundred twenty-five.

Most meditation apps begin the same way: sit up, relax your shoulders, find a quiet place. It sounds modern. It isn't. In the second chapter of the Shvetashvatara, more than two thousand years old by most estimates, there's a short set of instructions that reads almost like a checklist. Hold the body this way. Do this with the senses. Handle the breath like this. Pick a place like this. It is one of the earliest descriptions of sitting meditation anywhere in Hindu scripture, and it is surprisingly specific.
screen: `SIT UP. RELAX. FIND A QUIET PLACE.` → `NOT AN APP: AN UPANISHAD.` → `A CHECKLIST, CENTURIES OLD.`

segments.voice: Here is verse 2.8 in paraphrase. Holding the body steady, with the three upper parts upright, the chest, the neck and the head, and drawing the senses and the mind into the heart, the wise one crosses the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman. So: an upright body, and attention turned inward. Verse 2.9 takes the breath. Restrain the breath gently, with your movements quieted, and breathe out through the nose when the breath has grown soft. Then a famous image: hold the mind the way a driver holds a chariot yoked to wild horses, alert, never careless. Verse 2.10 chooses the place. Somewhere level and clean, free of pebbles, fire and sand. Pleasant to the mind, with the sound of water nearby. Nothing harsh to look at. Sheltered from the wind, tucked away. Read that list again and it's charmingly human. No sharp gravel under you. No smoke in your eyes. No wind blowing your attention around. The sacred begins with being comfortable enough to forget the body. The chariot image will sound familiar: the Katha Upanishad compared the senses to horses too. But here it is a working instruction, not just a parable. And the verses that follow promise small first signs of progress: lightness, health, a clear complexion, a pleasant voice. Teachers in many Hindu lineages still start students this way: spine straight, senses gathered, breath soft, a quiet place.
screen: `CHEST, NECK, HEAD: UPRIGHT.` · `BREATH SOFT, HORSES HELD.` · `A CLEAN, QUIET, SHELTERED PLACE.` · then, large: `THE BODY SET, THE MIND TURNS IN.`

segments.voice: Let's follow the checklist. Notice where you are: is it level, is anything sharp or noisy that you could move away from? Now sit, and stack the three: chest lifted, neck long, head balanced on top. Let the breath grow soft, and let it leave through the nose. Then gather the senses in, the way the verse says, as if the eyes, ears and skin were drawing back toward the heart. If a horse bolts, a thought, a sound, take the reins gently. The bell holds the time.
How to sit. The Shvetashvatara's instructions: upright from chest to head, senses drawn into the heart, breath soft, in a clean and quiet place.
Your line: the posture. Three times today, wherever you are, stack chest, neck and head, and take one soft breath out through the nose. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Hindus who meditate sit cross-legged or on a chair with the chest, neck and head in one line, choose a clean, quiet corner, and soften the breath before turning attention inward, much as Shvetashvatara 2.8–2.10 describes.

match.prompt: verse by verse: tap the pairs.
pairs: chest, neck and head held upright
the breath softened; the mind like wild horses
a clean, level, quiet, sheltered place
carries the meditator across the rivers

myth: the earliest Upanishads never describe how to sit
the Shvetashvatara gives a detailed instruction: upright body, senses drawn in, soft breath, a quiet place.
the text recommends a place with the sound of water nearby
2.10 lists pleasant sounds such as water among the signs of a good spot.
the verses that follow promise lightness and health as first signs
2.13 lists lightness, health, a clear complexion and a pleasant voice.

fork.setup: you want to start meditating, and you have three spots: a windy rooftop, a gravel path by a bonfire, a quiet room near running water. which would the Shvetashvatara pick?
options: the gravel path by the fire.
fork.reveal: 2.10 asks for a level, clean place, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasant to the mind, with water nearby, sheltered from wind.

original.note: Sanskrit āsana: seat, posture. the word the Yoga Sutras will later define as 'steady and comfortable'.

trapdoor: what you thought: posture is a modern add-on to old spiritual ideas.
what it means: one of the oldest Hindu meditation texts begins with the spine, the breath and the room.

what a scholar hears: Shvetashvatara 2.8–2.15 is among the earliest yoga instructions in the Upanishads, sharing vocabulary and images (the chariot, the breath) with the Katha and pointing toward Patanjali.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 2.8 (body upright, senses into the heart, the boat of Brahman)

notes: Date: 'more than two thousand years old by most estimates' (the Shvetashvatara is usually placed in the last centuries BCE). Confirm phrasing.
'One of the earliest descriptions of sitting meditation in Hindu scripture': widely stated; the Katha also has early yoga material. Please check.
2.10 list (pebbles, fire, sand/gravel; sound of water; not offensive to the eye; sheltered from wind) follows Müller/Hume; confirm.
